questions.q: What is a ballot drop box?
questions.a: A drop box is a secure, locked structure operated by election officials where voters can deliver their absentee ballot any time, day or night.

questions.q: Are drop boxes available in my state?
questions.a:
No, ballot drop boxes are not available in Delaware.

After you vote your absentee ballot (https://elections.delaware.gov/voter/absentee/pdfs/absentee_voting_instructions.pdf) you may return it by:

- Mailing it to the Department's office in your county (https://elections.delaware.gov/locations.shtml);
- Personally taking it to the Department's office in your county (https://elections.delaware.gov/locations.shtml); or
- Having someone take it to the Department's office in your county on your behalf

questions.q: Do I need an ID to register to vote in Delaware?
questions.a:
ID is not necessary to register to vote if you use the National Voter Registration Form (https://www.eac.gov/voters/national-mail-voter-registration-form/).

However, when registering with the Department of Elections or at an alternate approved location, current identification is required.

Accepted forms of ID

The identification must include current and valid photo ID that shows full name and address.

Examples include:

- Current utility bill
- Bank statement
- Government check
- Paycheck
- Other government document that shows full name and address
- Delaware Drivers License or State ID Card

questions.q: What if I don’t have an ID?
questions.a:
If you do not have one of the above types of ID, you can use the National Voter Registration Form (https://www.eac.gov/voters/national-mail-voter-registration-form/) when you register to vote.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: What voting assistance is available for voters with disabilities?
questions.a:
All people qualified to vote must be given the opportunity to do so. Therefore, there will be accessible polling places, accessible voting machines, the opportunity for voting by absentee ballot and assistance at any point as a means of accommodation.

If you need help at the polls, election officers are ready to assist. You may also bring someone with you to help in the voting process.

If you are deaf or hard of hearing, all election materials, announcements and forms are available at your  (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)state's election website (https://elections.delaware.gov). You may also use the state's free TDD relay service to obtain election and voting information. Simply dial 711 and give the operator the toll free help line number for the county from which you are calling: New Castle County 800-577-000, Kent County 800-464-4357, Sussex County 800-464-4357, Outside Delaware 800-273-9500.

questions.q: How do I request accommodation or report accessibility issues?
questions.a: If you have any questions about receiving help in voting, please ask the clerk or inspector at the polling place.

questions.q: Can I vote by mail because of my disability?
questions.a:
You may be able to vote by mail if you meet the eligibility requirements. You can learn more about the absentee ballot process here.  (https://www.vote411.org/delaware#absentee-ballot-process)

For more information, you can utilize the American Association of People With Disabilities (AAPD) (http://www.aapd.com/what-we-do/voting/) resource.

questions.q: What types of voting machines does Delaware use?
questions.a: The voting systems used in Delaware is DRE.

All the information about who and what you are voting for is on an electronic screen like a TV or computer screen.

There are many variations of DREs because lots of companies are inventing new ones, and many cities, counties and states are trying them out.

Usually, after you have signed in, the poll workers will give you a card that you slide into a device to start your voting session.

Some of these devices will show all of the candidates and ballot choices on one big screen. Often, with these big screen devices you push a button next to the name of the candidate you want to vote for (or yes or no on a ballot measure).

On other DREs, the screen is set up to show pages. On each screen or page, there will probably be one thing to vote on. For example, on one screen or page, you might vote for president. Then you might move to the next page to vote for senator. Often these small-screen devices have a touch screen, where you touch the screen next to the name of the person you want to vote for.

Other devices have a key pad. And some have a keyboard, so you can write in the name of someone you want to vote for.

You let the system know you are finished voting by pushing a button, touching the screen or entering something on a keypad.

You can learn more about voting systems by checking out the Elections Assistance Commission's (EAC) resource.  (https://www.eac.gov/voting-equipment/system-certification-process)
